substance:
The paper asks what structural condition on trustworthy data permits recovery of useful dataset properties after substantial arbitrary data have been added. Its central decision is to introduce a criterion called resilience, intended to support recovery of more than one kind of structure: the abstract explicitly names the mean and best low-rank approximation. The contamination setting concerns arbitrary additional observations, rather than merely random measurement noise. However, the supplied record does not specify the allowable contamination fraction, recovery accuracy, or formal definition of resilience.

The authors position resilience as weaker than most previously studied conditions while supporting a broader range of robust-estimation settings. This is a substantive assumption-design claim, not evidence that estimation becomes assumption-free. Without the definitions and comparisons, its breadth must remain the authors' characterization rather than an independently established conclusion about the literature.

The contribution list separates statistical possibility from computation. Information-theoretic results cover robust distribution learning, stochastic block model estimation, and mean estimation under bounded kth moments. Algorithmic results cover robust distribution learning and mean estimation in lp norms. That division matters: the abstract does not claim efficient algorithms for every setting in which it establishes recoverability, and it supplies neither rates nor runtime bounds.

A distinctive proof technique prunes a high-dimensional distribution having bounded first moments to obtain a stable core with bounded second moments. The analytical move is to discard part of a distribution to obtain stronger moment control on what remains, rather than assume second-moment control for the original distribution. The authors suggest that this technique may have independent usefulness. The supplied text does not specify retained mass, quantitative bounds, or subsequent applications, so neither the cost of pruning nor its broader effectiveness can be reconstructed.
attribution_limits: These are collective contributions and claims of the paper attributed to Jacob Steinhardt, Moses Charikar, and Gregory Valiant. First-author metadata does not identify who originated the criterion, proofs, or framing. Only an abstract and bibliographic record are supplied; no individual preference or historical change of mind is documented.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Weaker assumptions coexist with unspecified quantitative conditions. Information-theoretic recoverability must not be conflated with efficient computation. Extracting a bounded-second-moment core does not establish that the original distribution has bounded second moments. No contrary experimental findings are documented.
coverage_notes: Several evidence records repeat the same four abstract passages and count as one project, not independent support. The pruning result is noted as related to the first-moment improvement discussed in Learning from Untrusted Data; that relationship should not be counted as another independent research line. Metadata is not independently verified.

substance:
This project asks whether adversarial-example defenses can escape an evaluation cycle in which regularization or adversarial training appears successful until a stronger attack defeats it. The response is to seek a certificate covering an attack class rather than rely only on failures of particular attack algorithms. The investigation is explicitly restricted to neural networks with one hidden layer; the abstract does not establish extension to deeper architectures.

The first methodological component is a semidefinite relaxation that produces a certificate for a specified network and test input. Its purpose is to upper-bound the error an adversary can force within the modeled perturbation setting. Thus, the abstract's phrase 'no attack' concerns attacks satisfying the relevant constraints, not unrestricted adversarial actions against inputs, training data, or the surrounding system. The relaxation's derivation and full technical assumptions are unavailable.

The second component connects certification to model construction. Because the certificate is differentiable, the authors jointly optimize it with network parameters, using it as an adaptive robustness regularizer. Certification therefore serves both as an assessment mechanism and as a training signal. This is a concrete project-level integration of verification and optimization, not evidence that an individual author personally changed research priorities from evaluation to training.

The reported outcome is a network and certificate on MNIST for which perturbing each pixel by at most 0.1 cannot cause more than 35% test error. This is a certified upper bound, not an observed attack achieving 35% error, and not a guarantee of error-free classification. The result demonstrates a bounded robustness claim under a specified perturbation budget, while leaving substantial possible error. The supplied record contains no clean-accuracy comparison, runtime measurements, implementation details, or additional experimental conditions with which to assess practical tradeoffs.
attribution_limits: The motivation, architecture restriction, relaxation, training procedure, and MNIST result are collective work attributed to Aditi Raghunathan, Jacob Steinhardt, and Percy Liang. No passage assigns a particular decision or personal preference to Steinhardt. Evidence is abstract-level, and bibliographic metadata is unverified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The aspiration to end an attack–defense arms race is narrower in execution: one-hidden-layer networks, MNIST, and a specified pixelwise perturbation budget. A 35% certified error ceiling is neither the attained adversarial error nor comprehensive system safety. No clean-performance or computational-cost tradeoff can be determined.
coverage_notes: Repeated records reproduce the same motivation, certificate, training integration, and numerical result. They describe one project. This concerns adversarial perturbations at test time, not training-data poisoning.

substance:
The research question is whether out-of-distribution detection methods remain effective when evaluation moves beyond small, simple benchmarks toward larger and more varied visual tasks. The abstract motivates this gap through safety-relevant applications, including novel biological phenomena and self-driving cars. The collaborators operationalize greater realism through high-resolution images, thousands of classes, and different prediction structures, rather than merely increasing the number of examples in an otherwise unchanged classification task.

Three settings make that decision concrete. For ImageNet multiclass anomaly detection, the team introduces Species, containing over 700,000 images and more than a thousand anomalous species. For multilabel anomaly detection, it uses ImageNet-21K to evaluate detectors associated with PASCAL VOC and COCO. For spatial localization, it introduces a road-anomaly segmentation benchmark. These choices distinguish whole-image multiclass recognition, multilabel prediction, and pixel-level anomaly segmentation; the road task is not simply another collection of image-level outliers.

The principal reported comparative finding is that a surprisingly simple detector based on the maximum logit outperforms prior methods across all the evaluated large-scale multiclass, multilabel, and segmentation tasks. The authors consequently establish it as a baseline for subsequent work. The finding is important because expanded evaluation does not, in this record, support an assumption that greater detector complexity is necessary. It does not establish a personal preference for simple methods or universal superiority of maximum-logit scoring.

The benchmarks are presented as infrastructure enabling future research, not evidence of successful deployment in cars or biological discovery systems. The abstract supplies no numerical performance differences, uncertainty estimates, model configurations, comparator list, or ablations. Species filtering and overlap checks, the ImageNet-21K selection protocol, and the road benchmark's size and annotation process are also absent. Consequently, 'real-world' is an evaluation ambition supported by specified scale and task changes, not independently demonstrated deployment validity.
attribution_limits: All research choices and findings belong to the listed collaboration, including Hendrycks, Basart, Mazeika, Zou, Kwon, Mostajabi, Steinhardt, and Song. The abstract does not identify Steinhardt's role in dataset construction, baseline selection, or experimentation. Safety motivation is collective framing, not an individual priority statement.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The simple maximum-logit baseline reportedly beats prior methods, complicating any portrayal of this project as pursuing complexity for its own sake. Larger and more varied benchmarks do not by themselves establish real-world representativeness. No negative result for maximum-logit scoring is supplied, but comparative magnitudes and evaluation details are unavailable.
coverage_notes: Multiple evidence entries repeat the same three benchmark descriptions and comparative conclusion. Count them as one project. The unnamed road-anomaly benchmark should not be assigned a name from outside knowledge. Metadata is not independently verified.

substance:
This packet records an agenda-setting position paper, not an experimental demonstration of a safety technique. Its motivating question is what machine-learning safety research should address as systems become larger, acquire new capabilities, and enter high-stakes settings. The authors explicitly argue that safety should be a leading research priority, drawing an analogy with other powerful technologies. This is a collective normative recommendation grounded in their description of technological trends, not a measured comparison establishing safety's priority over every other field.

The principal concrete decision is to organize the research agenda around four hazard-oriented objectives. Robustness means withstanding hazards. Monitoring means identifying hazards. Alignment means reducing inherent model hazards. Systemic Safety means reducing systemic hazards. The distinctions preserve different targets of intervention: enduring a hazard is not identical to detecting it, and reducing hazards inherent in a model is not identical to reducing hazards at the systemic level. The framework therefore does not reduce all safety work to improving an individual model's robustness.

The authors describe these problems as ready for research and state that the paper clarifies their motivations and supplies concrete research directions. That is evidence of an intended connection between a broad safety argument and researchable problems. However, the supplied abstract does not contain those detailed directions. It cannot support attribution of particular experiments, algorithms, benchmarks, deployment procedures, or priorities within the four categories.

The contribution available for a later profile is consequently a shared safety-priority statement and an explicit organizational framework. There are no reported empirical outcomes, proof techniques, quantitative findings, failed interventions, or documented changes of mind in this record. The designation 'ready for research' is the authors' assessment of tractability, not evidence that these problems were solved or that the proposed directions were subsequently pursued successfully.
attribution_limits: The position and taxonomy are jointly attributed to Dan Hendrycks, Nicholas Carlini, John Schulman, and Jacob Steinhardt. They do not establish Steinhardt's individual ranking of research areas. Only the abstract and bibliographic record are supplied; the detailed proposed research is unavailable.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The paper calls safety a leading priority and presents four areas as research-ready, but this record supplies no evidence assessing their relative tractability, effectiveness, or resource requirements. No contrary position or negative research outcome is documented.
coverage_notes: The evidence consists of repeated versions of two passages, not six independent statements or completed projects. Decision evidence exists for agenda organization and collective prioritization, but not for concrete technical implementations. Metadata is unverified.

substance:
The project asks how to study training-induced behavioral changes outside a dataset's apparent domain when existing examples are scarce, hand-constructed, or accidental. Its motivating examples include broad misalignment following insecure-code training and a nineteenth-century persona following training on outdated bird names. These are cited motivations, not discoveries attributed to this project. The authors characterize the prior evidence as only dozens of isolated examples and respond by proposing automated discovery of datasets with surprising side effects, or DSSEs.

The discovery objective has three simultaneous requirements: elicit a target behavior, resemble ordinary post-training data, and surprise human auditors who inspect the data. This makes apparent ordinariness and difficult-to-anticipate effects explicit optimization targets rather than incidental observations. The pipeline operationalizes each objective with LLM judges and searches through evolution, reinforcement learning, and subliminal-learning approaches. The abstract does not supply scoring rubrics, thresholds, search budgets, or comparative evidence showing which search mechanism works best.

Candidate datasets are subsequently rescored and filtered using held-out metrics. The reported collection contains 6,575 DSSEs spanning eight behaviors, with many effects generalizing across model families and sizes. The filtering step distinguishes discovery scores from subsequent selection criteria, but the independence and definitions of the held-out metrics are unspecified. 'Many' provides no numerical transfer rate, and the eight behaviors are not enumerated in the supplied record.

The authors also compare automated assessments with human research judgments, reporting that their metrics track ML researchers' judgments and that frontier models outperform humans at predicting side effects in the study. This addresses whether automated surprise-related scores correspond to human assessments, while leaving participant selection, task conditions, effect sizes, and uncertainty unavailable. The collection is presented as a testbed for generalization research and groundwork for predicting training side effects before deployment. That prospective use is not evidence of an already validated deployment-screening procedure or broad model superiority over human researchers.
attribution_limits: The pipeline, objectives, collection, and comparisons are collective claims attributed to Yaowen Ye, Jacob Steinhardt, Sarah Schwettmann, and Cassidy Laidlaw. Motivating anecdotes belong to prior examples, not necessarily these authors. Only an abstract is supplied; no individual preference, role allocation, or human-evaluation protocol is available.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Human surprisingness is initially represented through model-judge proxies. Reported agreement with researchers provides a check, but without protocols or effect sizes it cannot establish comprehensive validity. Transfer is asserted for many datasets, not all, and predictive oversight before deployment remains an intended downstream use.
coverage_notes: Repeated entries describe one discovery project and one reported collection. Preserve the supplied 2026-11-04 bibliographic date as unverified metadata rather than independently established publication history. No exclusion reason is supplied for this otherwise usable abstract record.

substance:
ADAG asks how to make discovered circuits human-legible rather than equating circuit discovery with explanation. It automates tracing, attribution profiling, clustering, descriptions, and simulator-based checking. Experiments reuse a prior MLP-neuron tracing method; the framework is intended to be backbone-agnostic. Its RelP replacement changes backward computation while preserving forward behavior on the particular input, producing conservative input-times-gradient attribution—not global model equivalence.

To counter locality bias in activation exemplars and logit-lens descriptions, profiles combine dependence on preceding tokens with contributions to future logits. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, input tests sample 128 neurons per layer and 20 maximum-activating exemplars for positive and negative signs from 1,000 FineWeb documents truncated to 128 tokens. Eight preceding tokens explain neurons well only in the first three layers. A separate 100-document output test finds stronger nonlocality in early layers. Later-layer attribution concentrates on BOS, motivating its exclusion; attention sinks are a hypothesis, not an established cause.

Multiview spectral clustering combines clamped nonnegative input/output similarities by harmonic mean. Capitals-task ablations favor this choice for low contribution-sign mixing, balance, and cohesion, assessed through sign consistency, cluster-size variation, and silhouette scores. Separating opposing output effects aims to preserve steering effects. Separate explainers handle observed input tokens and hypothetical continuations. Candidates are selected by global Pearson correlation between measured scores and explanation-conditioned simulator predictions; quantile highlighting with minimum parameter one and twenty rather than five candidates improves this metric.

Validation uses previously interpreted city–state–capital circuits. For Dallas, zeroing the capital-city cluster changes the leading answer from Austin, initially 96.5%, to Texas at 93.4%; zeroing Dallas–Texas lowers Austin to 52.7% and raises Oklahoma to 22.1%. Medical analysis traces 150 jailbreak variants before generation into 20 supernodes, then zeroes or doubles neurons across positions on the base prompt. Fifty responses at temperature 0.7 are judged for harmful advice and coherence by Claude Haiku. Suppressing the pills-safety cluster raises attack success from 28% to 88%; amplifying the ridiculous-responsive cluster raises it to 90%.

Arithmetic tracing covers 10,000 addition examples, organized into 256 clusters and inspected through operand-grid heatmaps, including even-sum and approximate-sum patterns. Tracing takes about six hours on four GPUs. For 18 + 24, no individual zero/double intervention changes the leading answer, 42. Qwen3 32B replication requires adding Markdown bold syntax to the answer prefill and switching description models because compatible tokenizer-specific explainers are unavailable. Additional query–key, activation, and steering-effect views are explicitly deferred for time.
attribution_limits: All implementation decisions, design preferences, and findings are collective work attributed to Aryaman Arora, Zhengxuan Wu, Jacob Steinhardt, and Sarah Schwettmann; individual engineering contributions are not assigned. Prior tracing-method optimality and the inherited jailbreak dataset are reported from earlier work. The claim that LLMs will remain essential for translating reverse engineering into human understanding is a forward-looking authorial belief, not an experimentally established necessity. Embedded labeling prompts document the experiment, not personal speech or instructions to the reader.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The 'fully automated' framing retains manually chosen cluster counts. Simulator correlation is a proxy, not complete mechanistic validation. One expert received the same exemplars as the LLM; automatic descriptions scored similarly for inputs and higher for outputs, but used best-of-20 candidates and an LLM scorer. Most capitals ablations had little individual effect. Outside the strongest medical clusters, steering weakened and generally increased incoherence. C16's prevention of harmful responses may reflect impaired general instruction following rather than a safety mechanism; prose calls it 'medical pronouns' while the table calls it 'urgent medication reminders'. Medical scores use a different judge/model prompt from the source study. The arithmetic null result is limited to the displayed example and intervention strengths.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages describe one project. The main capitals graph retains only 50 inter-circuit edges and omits disconnected clusters; a fuller graph is supplied separately. Systems changes include replacing nnsight with torch hooks, removing unnecessary CUDA synchronization, batching gradients/Jacobians, data parallelism, sharding, NumPy vectorization, vLLM inference, and batched API calls. The addition timing uses four H100 80GB GPUs with per-GPU batch size four. Output-locality statistics concern the strongest contributor per layer, not all contributions. Claude Opus summarizes scored descriptions into short, concrete labels with inhibitory notation; no separate summary-fidelity score is established. Qwen replication uses a Claude Haiku fallback, so not every pipeline component is held constant.

substance:
The paper asks whether safety assessed for isolated models survives composition. Experiments test bounded, fixed automated adversaries; superhuman-model misuse is a motivating possibility, not a demonstrated setting. Safety means resistance under tested tasks and adversaries, not universal harmlessness. The mechanism combines a capable refusing model with a weaker, more compliant model without bypassing frontier safeguards. Manual decomposition serves vulnerable-code and explicit-image tasks; automated decomposition supplies benign intermediate solutions to a weaker final generator for hacking and simulated manipulation. Single-shot and single-model-decomposition baselines distinguish composition gains from decomposition alone.

Synthetic tasks target otherwise unmatched misuse questions and permit difficulty control. Claude 3 Opus was chosen for harder generated programming questions; prevention-framed requests yielded vulnerability specifications. The benchmark has 100 tasks, each with three vulnerabilities. GPT-4, excluded from assessed systems to reduce self-preference, judges both functionality and vulnerability. Avoiding expert labeling of 12,000 outputs is an explicit cost tradeoff. Llama 2 70B single-model decomposition scores 3.3%, versus 42.7% combined with Opus; these are judgments, not executed exploit tests.

Image tests use 100 prompts each for generic activities, unrealistic scenes such as lunch in space, and beach yoga, deliberately stressing unusual environments and poses. Prompts specify adults; illustrations are censored. Authors label pooled, shuffled images without generation-condition information, requiring quality, activity fidelity, and nudity. DALL-E 3 plus an InstructPix2Pix version of Stable Diffusion v1.5 reaches 30% on unrealistic scenes, versus at most 2% individually.

Hacking combinations reach approximately 22% GPT-4-assessed success; single-shot Mixtral reaches 11%, with other single-shot models below 4%. Mistral-family models respond 99% of the time while Claude Sonnet/Opus refuse at least 96%, partly separating capability failure from refusal. Llama 2 is omitted because intermediate solutions exceed its context capacity.

Manipulation is intentionally simulated to avoid manipulating people. GPT-4 models reactions from 100 disinformation-operation account histories, not genuine users. Experiments include 100 individual and 100 paired user–politician cases; paired targets increase difficulty. Mistral decomposition versus Opus combination yields 68.0% versus 71.7% for individuals and 25.3% versus 33.7% for pairs. Long prompts and rate limits restrict this study to Opus/Mistral 7B.

The authors recommend lifecycle reassessment as new systems create combinations, while weighing beneficial and harmful uses together. They report sharing findings with frontier labs and releasing comparatively weak methods; publication's preventive value and future agent/fine-tuning risks are arguments, not measured outcomes.
attribution_limits: The study, release decisions, and deployment recommendations are collective work attributed to Erik Jones, Anca Dragan, and Jacob Steinhardt. The record does not identify which authors labeled images, chose particular models, or used writing tools. Code outcomes are model-evaluated; image outcomes are author-labeled; manipulation outcomes are simulated preferences of artificial profiles. None establishes individual personal preferences or demonstrated persuasion of real people.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Synthetic questions have qualitatively lower diversity; intermediate success rates do not establish representative coverage. Large code-score gaps and no optimization against GPT-4 support the authors' qualitative-confidence argument but are not expert validation. Equal evaluator error across conditions is assumed rather than demonstrated; human image results corroborate a different domain. Refusal measurements use output-format proxies. Llama 7B sometimes outperforms 13B in combinations, attributed to refusal differences; stronger-frontier advantages in hacking are within the margin of error for Mistral. Some single-model decomposition results exceed the quoted single-shot figures. Strong jailbreaks were not exhaustively tested and might outperform combinations. Adult-only prompts are a constraint, not an audited guarantee. Publication still creates acknowledged misuse risk.
coverage_notes: Repeated extracts describe one four-task project. Manipulation histories contain at least 39 tweets per account and come from accessible Russian-disinformation accounts, selected partly for privacy and access reasons; adversarial generators were not told users were simulated. Tens-of-thousands-token prompts and days of API-limited testing restricted model coverage. Language sampling uses temperature 0.01 because some APIs interpret zero adaptively, with task-specific token budgets. Image guidance 7.7/1.3 beat 7.5/1.5 across methods and baselines; only two settings were compared. The authors disclose GPT-4 sentence advice and DALL-E figure icons, without assigning individual tool use. No disclosure recipients, timing, or mitigation-effectiveness measurements are supplied.

substance:
The paper asks how to learn utility-sensitive decisions when experts cannot reliably specify a full objective and the learner's decision class is misspecified. Stop-sign versus postbox mistakes motivate unequal costs; a three-cluster construction gives two predictors identical 1/3 classification error but different utility. Utilities may be arbitrary [0,1]-valued functions, but add across instances. Proper learners compete with the best member of a restricted decision class, not unrestricted optimal behavior. The main exposition uses binary decisions.

Single-context comparisons reveal rankings but not cross-context mistake costs. Comparing whole decision functions would shift an enormous burden to humans, illustrated by comparing a million simultaneous predictions. The proposed k-comparison instead compares cumulative utilities of two decision bundles across k inputs. Larger k supplies finer information at greater presumed elicitation difficulty; the paper studies accuracy and query counts, not measured human effort.

The plug-in strategy estimates utilities only at sampled points, then maximizes empirical estimated utility. Generalization depends on the decision class composed with the fixed true utility, avoiding uniform learning of every bounded utility. If the class fits sampled optimal labels, the additional utility-ignorance term vanishes, but statistical error remains. For binary decisions, only correct-versus-incorrect utility gaps need estimation.

Comptron maintains symbolic gaps relative to the largest sampled gap, exploiting invariance to positive rescaling. Coordinate-wise perceptron-style updates retain consistent estimates and decrease contradicted ones. An interval-halving invariant gives maximum gap error at most twice the largest gap divided by k using O(n log k) queries; the stated schedule is log2(k)−1 rounds. Rob-Comptron averages repeated responses under query-dependent error uniformly bounded by eta<1/2. Hoeffding concentration and a union bound recover deterministic updates with high probability, at roughly (1−2eta)−2 query overhead plus logarithmic factors.

To isolate information limits, the lower bound grants the input distribution and a noiseless oracle. Two indistinguishable utilities on a two-point linear-class construction favor different decisions, yielding an Omega(1/k) worst-case penalty matching the plug-in rate. Yet Comptron is not instance-adaptive: a construction with gaps 1, 4/k, and 2/k² estimates the smallest as 2/k. Comparing it with the intermediate gap instead gives an 8/k² upper estimate and can change the selected decision.

The response is randomized robust optimization over all oracle-consistent utilities, characterizing local difficulty by instability of optimal decisions. Detailed upper and lower moduli nearly match rather than coincide. The finite-sample extension uses all comparisons, costing O(n^k) queries versus O(n log k); it sketches a local-modulus-plus-generalization bound. Efficient instance adaptation remains open, and this construction does not prove exhaustive querying necessary.
attribution_limits: The framework, algorithms, counterexamples, and theoretical claims are collaborative work attributed to Kush Bhatia, Peter L. Bartlett, Anca D. Dragan, and Jacob Steinhardt. Human utility-specification difficulty is cited motivation, not a reported human-subject finding. Algorithmic correction and stopping rules are not evidence of personal debugging habits or research stopping preferences. The exposition's move from minimax to instance analysis does not establish a chronological change of mind.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Unrestricted bounded utilities still require additive aggregation, oracle access, and decision-class/sampling conditions. Increasing comparison order may worsen human bias or noise, but that interaction is left open. The noisy guarantee does not cover arbitrary correlated errors or systematic errors at or above one half. Proposition 1's supplied statements/proof have estimate-direction and notation inconsistencies. Proposition 2 states a broader k range than the appendix's displayed k>10 argument; its exact 1/k counterexample equality is therefore not independently validated here. Rounding the iteration schedule for arbitrary k is unspecified. Overview language calling the robust estimator instance-optimal is stronger than literal equality of its distinct upper and lower local moduli. O(n^k) is exponential in k, not in n when k is fixed.
coverage_notes: Numerous repeated extracts represent one theoretical project, not independent replications. Related-work positioning connects k-comparisons to incomplete preferences and lottery granularity 1/k, while distinguishing this setting from nuisance-parameter approaches with direct utility-value access and restricted learnable utility classes. The criticism of misspecification applies to the realizable approaches described, not all inverse reinforcement learning or revealed-preference methods. No empirical implementation, human elicitation study, or globally efficient decision-optimization guarantee should be inferred from oracle-query bounds.

substance:
Steinhardt evaluates both the accuracy of AI-progress forecasts and whether successful probabilities rested on sound technical reasoning. He commissioned forecasts for four benchmarks at annual June 30 resolution dates from 2022 through 2025; this retrospective concentrates on MATH and MMLU. After first-year underprediction, including his own anecdotal impressions, he registered personal forecasts in July 2022. The target was the highest credibly claimed, eligible benchmark accuracy by June 30, 2023, with restrictions on training data—not latent capability irrespective of documentation.

Reported resolutions were 69.6% on MATH and 86.4% on MMLU, respectively his 41st and 66th percentiles. He therefore slightly overpredicted MATH and underpredicted MMLU, and informally rated the more bullish, same-date Metaculus forecast slightly above himself. Hypermind’s successful, narrower MATH prediction did not offset its severe MMLU tail miss, particularly after earlier misses. His prior objection to its 72.5% MMLU median invoked a possible Minerva–Chinchilla combination yielding 74.2%, an anticipated combination rather than an observed result.

His assessment of experts changed: formally elicited XPT predictions looked better than generalist forecasts, reversing his earlier informal impression. He became more optimistic about expert forecasting with training and incentives, while considering selection, effort, submission timing, and awareness of Minerva as competing explanations. Because XPT’s 2024 and 2030 forecasts were unresolved, he used achieved performance, trend continuation, and a newer Metaculus distribution as provisional diagnostics, not realized scores.

The mechanism audit combines aggregate trends with candidate improvements in aggregation, fine-tuning data, chain-of-thought, training allocation, model size, and data processing. He hypothesized that formatting-oriented solution distillation in Let’s Verify Step by Step improved accuracy, citing analogous GSM-8K gains from 74% to 82%. However, he had mainly anticipated inference-time chain-of-thought gains, omitted additional pretraining data, and overlooked regression on individual dimensions such as reduced math fine-tuning. An approximately ten-point aggregation improvement existed but was ineligible because of disallowed training data. For MMLU, GPT-4’s five-shot result without benchmark-specific fine-tuning supported his prediction of general-purpose improvements; plausible but undocumented enhancements did not count.

His resulting checklist separates data growth from model growth, permits backward movement on particular axes, and considers both hidden implementation gains and available techniques nobody applies. He resists hindsight certainty about the conjunction of GPT-4’s release and specialized follow-up research, qualifies his favorable self-assessment with N=2, and explicitly encourages experts and superforecasters to register public predictions.
attribution_limits: Commissioning, registering forecasts, revising judgments, and auditing reasoning are explicitly Steinhardt’s statements. Benchmark achievements and other groups’ forecasts are reported external results, not his experiments. His attribution of approximately eight percentage points to distillation and two to additional pretraining data is a retrospective hypothesis, not an ablation. Proposed effects of incentives, calibration practice, and hidden training techniques are beliefs rather than established causes. Public registration is an explicit recommendation; broader personal preferences need not be inferred.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The expert comparison changes populations, elicitation conditions, and information availability; some comparisons concern unresolved forecasts. His 2024 MATH upper percentile of 97.5%, versus experts’ 95%, looked more defensible under the Metaculus proxy but did not establish superior eventual calibration. That proxy is another forecast, not reality. GPT-4’s undisclosed pretraining, possible arXiv exposure, and better filtering prevent clean attribution of gains or losses from fewer fine-tuning tokens. His numerical success coexists with mechanism mistakes, and MMLU scaling gains were somewhat underestimated. Two outcomes and an informal crowd ranking cannot establish durable forecasting skill.
coverage_notes: Numerous evidence records repeat the same passages and decisions; they constitute one retrospective, not independent replications. The supplied evidence flags an apparent year-label inconsistency in the Metaculus proxy description. Only two of the original four benchmark targets are substantively covered here. Future checklist adoption and later forecast resolutions are not supplied.

substance:
This packet documents an editorial experiment rather than Steinhardt’s research findings about an AI-development pause. In his introductory host text, he says he is experimenting with guest posts to represent additional viewpoints, particularly ideas from researchers who do not already have a platform. The concrete decision is to publish Nora Belrose’s essay as the first guest selection described in the evidence. His stated aim concerns who gains visibility and which arguments readers encounter; the record does not establish the experiment’s duration, uptake, or subsequent effects.

Steinhardt gives a specific selection rationale: he considers the essay an example of independent thinking on a complicated, polarizing issue and finds some of its arguments original and interesting. He identifies two examples explicitly as Belrose’s beliefs: that robustness and alignment may be at odds, and that stochastic gradient descent may be safer than most alternative training algorithms. These examples identify what attracted his editorial attention, but the supplied introductory evidence does not provide their derivations, experiments, or empirical support. It would therefore be inappropriate to reconstruct a technical finding from these short descriptions.

His publication threshold is deliberately distinct from full agreement: hosting means he regards a viewpoint as worth engaging with, not that he accepts all its arguments. This supports a bounded, explicit editorial preference for intellectual independence and discussable originality in this selection. It does not establish his own position on pausing AI, his comparative assessment of training algorithms, or a personal belief that robustness conflicts with alignment. Nor does the disclaimer establish disagreement with any particular claim. The useful profile evidence is the communication decision and its articulated boundary, not the substantive conclusion suggested by the guest essay’s title.
attribution_limits: Only the introductory host text is individual evidence about Jacob Steinhardt. The main essay is by Nora Belrose despite metadata listing Steinhardt as sole author. Anti-pause arguments, the robustness–alignment tension, and comparative SGD safety must remain attributed to Belrose. Steinhardt explicitly endorses engagement with the viewpoint, not every conclusion.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Publishing an anti-pause essay can superficially look like endorsement, but his explicit disclaimer prevents that inference. Conversely, the disclaimer does not reveal which arguments he rejects or accepts. No technical experiment, policy evaluation, or outcome of the guest-hosting initiative is documented.
coverage_notes: The nine evidence records repeat three introductory passages. They support one editorial choice, not nine independent observations. Relevance is primarily research communication and editorial selection rather than technical methodology or a settled AI-policy position. Metadata authorship is misleading for the main essay.

substance:
ETHICS asks whether pretrained models possess contextual knowledge of everyday moral judgments across justice, deontology, virtue ethics, utilitarianism, and commonsense morality. The collaborative project deliberately draws on multiple philosophical traditions rather than equating machine ethics with fairness or one preferred theory. Its more than 130,000 examples are intended to measure, not install, ethical knowledge. Supervised and self-supervised representations are pursued as a route toward transferable preferences, not as an already demonstrated general ethical decision system.

Collection emphasizes clear-cut scenarios under ordinary background assumptions, treating the text as containing essential information. Qualified crowdworkers received reference examples; independent relabeling removed disagreements. Justice, deontology, and commonsense examples generally required four-of-five agreement; virtue traits required unanimity among three annotators; utility sets required seven annotators’ majority agreement on every adjacent comparison, with ranking presentation randomized. Initial contributors were English speakers in the US, Canada, and Great Britain. Long Reddit examples required at least 100 votes and 95% agreement, with highly political or sexual material excluded.

Task design makes contextual distinctions concrete. Impartiality pairs two reasonable and two unreasonable explanations for unequal treatment. Virtue examples use minimally edited scenarios and independently supplied distractor traits. Deontology tests exemptions from requests and responsibilities associated with roles. Utility models independently score scenarios but learn and are evaluated through pairwise pleasantness rankings: absolute regression was rejected because utility scale is not uniquely fixed and coarse ratings poorly distinguish nearby cases. Annotation adopts a typical-US-person perspective. GPT-3 instead receives an explicitly arbitrary 1–10 rating prompt to preserve independent scenario processing.

Contrast examples and adversarial filtering target superficial cues. Hard Test construction ranks losses from distil-BERT and distil-RoBERTa over five repeated splits. Justice, deontology, and virtue require every related example to be correct; other tasks use classification or pairwise ordering. Fine-tuned transformers were compared with few-shot GPT-3 and GloVe word averaging. Larger models improved, but the best Hard Test average was 47.9%; GPT-3 was relatively more competitive there than on ordinary Test examples. GloVe’s inferior performance despite much larger pretraining token counts challenges a token-volume-only explanation without isolating architecture’s effect.

Diagnostics revealed framing sensitivity, nonmonotonic monetary rankings, universal death ranked above a severe individual accident, and a name substitution flipping a wrongness prediction from 55% to 46%. A separate roughly 1,000-example contentious set tested disagreement recognition; uncertainty-based AUROCs of 58%, 69%, and 56% were weak. These results expose limits beyond aggregate accuracy. The authors also disclose normal-Test hyperparameter selection and best-over-runs reporting, limiting an untouched-holdout interpretation.
attribution_limits: All design choices, normative arguments, and findings are collective work; Steinhardt’s coauthorship does not establish his individual contribution or personal ethical commitments. Model utility values and wrongness probabilities are outputs, not ground-truth welfare quantities or researchers’ confidence in moral propositions. The argument that researchers cannot delegate contextual legal understanding entirely to policymakers is a collective normative position. Chatbot steering, sequential decision-making, broader stakeholder engagement, individualized values, explainability, and comprehensive adversarial or distribution-shift validation are proposed extensions, not completed deployments.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The shared-values framing is narrower than global representation: consensus filtering, Western English-speaking collection, a typical-US utility perspective, and Reddit selection all constrain coverage. Reddit vote counts were inferred from comment upvotes rather than a representative survey. Ten Indian annotators per short commonsense example produced 93.9% agreement with US labels, but this limited check does not establish universality; explanations involving idioms or misunderstandings remain conjectural. Mixed task metrics have different chance levels, and fine-tuning versus few-shot adaptation confounds model comparisons. Hardness is relative to the filtering models. The utility model lacked a reject option even for meaningless input. Diagnostic errors are illustrative, not prevalence estimates; the name-change mechanism remained unexplained. Best-over-runs reporting leaves ambiguity about whether the same run determines both test scores.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one ETHICS project and must not multiply its evidential weight. The datasheet excludes moral dilemmas and substantially disputed scenarios from the main benchmark’s intended use; the contentious subset tests disagreement detection separately. Collection forms and a datasheet support procedural reuse, but raw data were not saved, preprocessing software was unavailable at the time, and no updates were then planned. Results concern the models in this paper version, not present-day capability.

substance:
Steinhardt frames agent oversight as a practical inspection problem: systems that invoke language models across multiple turns, use tools, and retain state can generate transcripts containing hundreds of thousands of tokens. The research question is how to make those trajectories useful for diagnosing failures rather than relying only on an aggregate task score. He presents Docent as a Transluce team-built system intended to accelerate transcript analysis and surface corrupted tasks, scaffolding problems, unexpected behavior, and capability weaknesses.

The strongest concrete example concerns evaluation infrastructure. Docent identified packages that GPT-4o attempted to invoke but that were missing from its environment. Adding those packages reportedly increased InterCode solve rate from 68.6% to 78%, a 9.4-percentage-point change. The intervention described is environmental repair, not an improvement to model weights. Steinhardt explicitly connects this result to the use of benchmarks such as InterCode in assessing cyberrisk and other societal impacts. The example makes a particular interpretive distinction useful: an observed failure can reflect an unavailable dependency rather than, or alongside, a limitation in the agent’s underlying ability.

A second example illustrates qualitative behavioral inspection. After repeatedly failing a task, GPT-4o generated nonsense about “chestnut facts” and attempted to “re-examine for latent conceptual derivation.” Steinhardt uses this trajectory to show that transcript analysis can reveal unexpected behavior beyond missing dependencies or final success rates. The language is the model’s output, not his reasoning or terminology.

The supplied overview establishes a released tool, a reported debugging intervention, and an illustrative anomaly. It does not expose Docent’s internal analysis method, quantify inspection-time savings, compare it systematically with manual review, or establish how frequently either failure type occurs. Its distinctive contribution here is connecting trajectory inspection to both benchmark interpretation and behavioral understanding, with evidence strongest for the specific environment repair rather than broad effectiveness claims.
attribution_limits: Steinhardt explicitly supplies the oversight framing and explains why the InterCode correction matters. Docent’s construction is attributed to the Transluce team, with no individual implementation allocation. The solve-rate comparison is a reported project result. The anomalous phrases belong to GPT-4o and must not be treated as researcher speech, personal stopping behavior, or evidence of an internal model motive.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The positive benchmark change lacks sample sizes, uncertainty estimates, and a full comparison protocol in this short post. Claims of rapid or automatic analysis are not accompanied by a comprehensive tool evaluation. The failure-trajectory example has neither a prevalence estimate nor a causal explanation; it does not establish a general syndrome of behavior after failure.
coverage_notes: The twelve records repeat four substantive passages from one short project overview. The linked full write-up and video contents are not supplied and cannot fill methodological gaps. Transcript length is a stated motivation, not a systematic measurement of oversight capacity.

substance:
Steinhardt investigates historical human catastrophes and species extinctions as reference classes for AI risk. He distinguishes stories’ value for communicating concrete dangers—including his own earlier scenarios—from their weakness as forecasts: particular narratives are improbable and simplify multicausal reality. Base rates are meant to clarify which properties of AI warrant departure from precedent, not erase genuine novelty. He also warns that numerical history can be conjectural and describes extensive reading to decide which estimates to trust.

For human events, he scraped Wikipedia lists of wars, slavery and forced labor, famines, epidemics, and natural disasters into a Pandas dataframe with a shared Python script. Catastrophes require deaths equal to at least 0.1% of world population at the event’s start; a strict subset requires at least 1% mortality and duration under a decade. Other technological-disaster lists had smaller tolls; genocides were generally excluded to avoid overlap with wars. Starting in 1500, he reports 51 catastrophes and 11 strict catastrophes, approximately 0.11 and 0.02 per year.

Apparent increases across categories, including famines, motivate concern about historical underreporting and his later starting window. Reported Ljung-Box and Wald-Wolfowitz tests for 1500–1900 did not reject the stated temporal null, with p-values 0.36 and 0.26. These results do not establish a constant rate. An approximately inverse-severity relationship above 1% mortality supports extrapolation to larger events, but fails below that threshold; log-normal severity and missing smaller events remain alternative explanations. Examples involving climate, famine, disease, unrest, and policy lead him to recommend addressing upstream systemic contributors alongside immediate mechanisms.

He narrows extinction analysis to the Late Quaternary and Holocene to mitigate fossil-sampling, species-transition, and event-aggregation difficulties. After reading competing accounts, he follows Koch and Barnosky’s systematic review for human-versus-climate explanations and Barnosky and colleagues’ 2011 estimates for their treatment of sampling bias. The resulting synthesis treats humans as central while retaining regional climate contributions. He also asks why threats usually fail to cause extinction: coevolved defenses and predator population feedback constrain danger, whereas novel predators sustained by alternative prey can evade those limits.

AI’s potential adaptation, replication, and coordination concern him, but other technologies’ historical record and possible AI benefits for famine, climate, and prosperity lower his assessment. He separates a roughly 5% historical estimate for a catastrophe killing 10% of humanity within 25 years from his personal additional ten-percentage-point AI forecast, whose justification is deferred. Temporal change, technology’s contribution, intelligence as a cause of others’ extinction, and alternative exposure measures such as GDP doublings remain unresolved.
attribution_limits: Dataset construction, thresholds, source selection, grouping choices, and the AI-specific forecast are explicitly Steinhardt’s. Historical mortality estimates and extinction findings come from external sources; his ecological account is synthesis, not original biological experimentation. Addressing upstream causes is his stated recommendation, not an evaluated intervention. The additional AI risk is a dated personal forecast, not a statistical output of the historical dataset, and its promised justification is unavailable here.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Despite excluding genocides to reduce overlap, the Taiping Rebellion remains counted as both war and famine. Post-1500 restriction does not eliminate reporting bias; population estimates, death tolls, event boundaries, and sparse data remain uncertain. The named tests’ non-rejections do not establish identical distributions or stationarity, and he ultimately calls temporal variation inconclusive. His preferred Holocene source gives lower estimates than some alternatives without settling that disagreement. Ecological analogies do not directly measure AI risk. He still uses a simplified extinction story while explicitly acknowledging that it suppresses uncertainty. Evidence that intelligent mammals survived extinction is not evidence that they caused other species’ extinction.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages describe one analysis. A separate recoding of Hoffmann and colleagues’ endangerment figure grouped causes into habitat destruction, invasive species including chytrid fungus, overhunting/overfishing, and environment; ambiguous categories make those counts approximate. Species and genera are partly simplified together. The 25-year forecast concerns 10% population loss, not human extinction. Alternative clocks based on population, economic growth, or technological progress are considered but not adopted.

substance:
This collaborative project asks whether language models can provide scalable, reasoned probability forecasts through retrieval, reasoning, and aggregation. The team curated binary questions using automated screening followed by manual removal of ambiguous or low-engagement items, converting multiple-choice questions where appropriate. It compared forecasts with historical platform crowd aggregates and used Brier score for its incentive to report genuine probabilities. Fourteen no-retrieval baselines reached a best score of 0.208 versus the crowd’s 0.149.

Retrieval changed when straightforward query expansion missed relevant considerations: election polling searches were supplemented with decomposition covering campaign finance, economics, and geopolitics. Five date-bounded news APIs were compared on 24 unresolved questions; Google News and NewsCatcher were selected. Manual inspection rejected title-only relevance filtering because plausible titles could accompany failed scrapes or paywall errors. GPT-3.5 scoring of titles plus the first 250 words achieved 0.73 recall and 0.65 precision against full-text GPT-4 judgments on 169 articles, with approximately 70% cost savings. Downstream validation Brier scores favored 15 relevance-ranked summaries; 20 performed similarly.

Reasoning prompts rephrase questions, generate and weight arguments for both outcomes, and check confidence and base rates. GPT-4-1106-Preview outperformed Claude-2.1 by 0.01–0.03 Brier points for inference, although Claude contributed useful training candidates. Two retrieval configurations, four prompts, and two models generated 16 candidate forecasts per question/date. Selection retained outputs beating the crowd’s realized Brier score, but discarded deviations exceeding 0.15 and averaged retained probabilities with crowd estimates to counter selection-induced overconfidence. Scratchpad instructions were omitted from training inputs to encourage context-dependent reasoning selection. Of 73,632 reasonings, 13,253 qualified; budget and availability limited GPT-4-0613 fine-tuning to the newest 6,000 for two epochs.

The final ensemble combines three base-model and three fine-tuned forecasts, halving and redistributing the weight of the prediction furthest from the median. This modified trimmed mean won a small validation comparison; model-based universal self-consistency did not improve the baseline, and post-hoc binning or isotonic calibration brought no gain.

Full-test Brier score improved to 0.179 but remained worse than the crowd’s 0.149; accuracy was 71.5% versus 77%. A validation-derived policy requiring crowd probability 0.3–0.7, one of the first three retrieval dates, and at least five relevant articles achieved 0.240 versus 0.247, retaining 22% of forecasts and 43% of questions. A four-to-one crowd/model blend improved full-test Brier score to 0.146. Removing fine-tuning yielded 0.186; removing retrieval too yielded 0.206, limiting claims for prompt optimization alone. Thus the evidence supports substantial improvement and modest complementarity, not unrestricted human-level superiority.
attribution_limits: Methods, findings, and motivations belong to the coauthored project, not individually identified decisions or private preferences of Steinhardt. Experimental scratchpad instructions are not evidence of his personal reasoning routine. Generated explanations are inspectable outputs, not proven faithful accounts of internal computation. Safety training as a cause of refusal or hedging is explicitly hypothetical. Iterative self-supervision until training data are exhausted, domain-adaptive training motivated by knowledge correlations, and interactive assistance to human forecasters are proposed future work. Budget-limited training is not a general personal stopping rule.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Temporal controls are substantial but not conclusive. Most descriptions place test questions after June 1, 2023 and training/validation resolutions before it; another passage says 2024, and some model cutoffs are unknown or inconsistent with the blanket guarantee. Final evaluation uses five geometrically spaced opening-to-closing dates, dropping post-resolution dates, but tuning uses opening-to-resolution midpoints despite warning that resolution-relative scheduling leaks outcome-correlated information. This does not establish that final tests used midpoint dates. Timestamp whitelists and exclusion of comment URLs do not rule out later article edits; twenty-event knowledge probes cannot prove no contamination. Reported standard errors likely understate dependence-related uncertainty. GPT-4 relevance labels are not human ground truth. Underconfidence coexists with overconfidence: the model assigned 20% to McCarthy resigning by the same-day deadline versus the crowd’s 1%, but assigned 95% to Barbie earning twice Oppenheimer’s opening gross versus 73% from the crowd after treating projections as facts; both resolved no. Original retrieved prompts are not shown. GPT-3.5 substitution used more training examples than GPT-4, sometimes retained base GPT-4 forecasts, and has a 0.181/0.182 reporting discrepancy.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project and dataset release. The raw collection contained 48,754 questions; curated splits contained 3,762 training, 840 validation, and 914 test questions from Metaculus, Good Judgment Open, INFER, Polymarket, and Manifold. Platform crowd aggregation differs, and Metaculus’s crowd forecast is distinct from its proprietary prediction. Optimization used sequential small hyperparameter groups, relevance proxies for query generation, and refusal frequency to break similar baseline prompt scores; the relevance prompt and discard threshold of three were left untuned. Selective results require crowd access; early-date and article-count filters individually did not beat the crowd, and some early-retrieval statistics conflict between prose and table. Category comparisons are explicitly cautioned as noisy.

substance:
This collaboration asks why gradient-trained attention acquires particular alignments when equally accurate models can attend differently. Its two-stage approximation proposes that word co-occurrence first teaches knowledge to translate individual words (KTIW), which subsequently guides attention. A lexical probe measures correct-output probability when attention concentrates on one encoder state; interpreting this as isolated word knowledge requires locality. The tractable proxy replaces contextual states with embeddings, averages them under uniform attention, removes the decoder state, and uses a linear softmax output. Under Gaussian initialization, gradient flow, and an infinite-dimensional limit, its initial gradient yields IBM Model 1's co-occurrence count table—not equivalent full trajectories.

Translation and classification experiments compare the highest-scoring position with the other quantity's top 5%, contextualizing agreement through a separately initialized model's training performance. Token accuracy avoids compounded autoregressive errors; BLEU and Kendall correlation provide alternative views. Freezing attention uniformly still permits lexical probes agreeing with ordinary attention above chance. Conversely, training only attention with everything else frozen yields weaker agreement, even at its best validation checkpoint.

A targeted copying distribution permutes the same 40 word types in every example: the bag-of-words proxy cannot learn, and the full model sometimes fails or learns slowly. Sampling 40 words from 60 preserves length while restoring informative variation and succeeds across twenty reported seeds. A mixture of two disjoint 40-word vocabularies supplies group information without positional discrimination, likewise producing difficulty rather than universal full-model impossibility. Rejection-sampled eight-head models fail with all individually unsuccessful initializations but converge with one successful initialization, supporting an optimization—not expressiveness—explanation in this toy setup.

The paper also demonstrates where its explanation breaks. In balanced length-40 keyword detection, prolonged uniform-attention training shifts useful information toward the final state; log-odds expose differences obscured by saturated probabilities. Copying reaches perfect accuracy within 300 iterations while a fixed positional permutation fails despite identical uniform-attention probe behavior, implicating attention-network inductive biases. A three-output counterexample assigns optimal attention zero weight at the largest lexical score. A modified translation architecture permitting convex attention optimization with other quantities fixed achieves 38.2 versus 37.9 BLEU and reports lexical/optimal-attention agreement of 0.53. The attraction relationship remains a heuristic, not a theorem or guarantee of faithful saliency explanations. The authors advocate intuitive concepts combined with formal trajectory reasoning, while warning against treating their framework as interpretability ground truth in medicine or recidivism.
attribution_limits: All technical decisions, interpretations, warnings, and future aspirations are statements of the coauthored paper, not independently attributable choices or private preferences of Steinhardt. Changes during training describe models, not changes in his beliefs. Findings concern the evaluated recurrent architectures and synthetic settings; the toy multi-head result does not establish why modern transformers generally benefit from multiple heads. Metadata authorship order and date are not independently verified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Uniform-attention agreement rises and then falls, so the paper reports its maximum over training rather than its final value. The authors assess inflation as minimal, but the supplied evidence provides no independent selection correction. The reverse intervention also selects maximum validation agreement and freezes much more than an isolated lexical-knowledge variable. SMS Spam Collection was excluded from main tables because attention varied substantially across seeds; its short sequences, small dataset, and small vocabulary are possible context, not established causes, and investigation was deferred. Logistic-regression/proxy comparisons differ in regularization and retraining seeds, so equivalent binary model classes need not produce identical fitted results.
coverage_notes: Many records repeat the same passages and experiments; they constitute one project, not independent confirmations. Evaluation includes Multi30K, IWSLT'14, News Commentary language pairs, and six classification datasets including IMDB, AG News, 20 Newsgroups, SST, Amazon, and Yelp. Classification training used batch size 32 for 4,000 iterations, with dense early checkpoints. The binary proxy's factorization is not rank-limiting; the logistic baseline's L2 coefficient was selected by validation accuracy across ten orders of magnitude. The paper credits Sun and Lu (2020) with nearly identical high-level binary-classification arguments and a subtler analysis. Appendix metrics are alternate analyses, not replications.

substance:
The study asks whether aggregate gains from larger pretrained models conceal regressions on individual examples. Single-run comparisons are inadequate: two BERT-base finetuning seeds disagree on 8% of instances despite only 0.1% accuracy difference. The authors therefore define instance accuracy as expected correctness over pretraining and finetuning randomness, estimating it with ten independently pretrained models and five finetuning runs each, across five BERT sizes and MNLI, QQP, and SST-2. Measuring pretraining variation required training their own checkpoints. To afford replication, they shortened context from 512 to 128 and increased pretraining from one to two million steps. Comparisons with original releases preserved aggregate scaling trends, but their base and large models were 2–3% worse on MNLI.

Their decay estimator compares the negative tail of large-minus-small instance accuracy with a baseline formed by splitting models into groups containing equal mixtures of both sizes. The maximum excess over thresholds estimates a lower bound on the fraction that worsens. Crucially, the theorem concerns fixed-threshold expectations under independence, not a high-probability confidence guarantee. Recognizing dependence among finetuning runs sharing a checkpoint, the authors changed the target to five-run finetuning ensembles within each pretraining seed. The MNLI mini-to-large estimate consequently fell from roughly 6% to 4%, against a 10% aggregate improvement. A counterexample demonstrates why the original independence argument can fail; bootstrap analyses separately assess threshold-selection optimism.

The project initially used Fisher's exact test with Benjamini–Hochberg, then developed a procedure detecting decay with two rather than ten pretraining seeds in the reported comparisons. The estimated 80% compute saving is retrospective, not realized. The competing procedure's false-discovery parameter was optimized to avoid handicapping it.

A blinded audit sampled decay and control examples with equal probability, using Correct, Fine, Wrong, and Unsure categories. The first author annotated 100 examples per task; the second reproduced the qualitative finding. Problematic labels were enriched among regressions but did not explain them all. Manual inspection found no coherent semantic pattern among correctly labeled regressions.

Two further analyses address misleading summaries. Conditioning successive gains on middle-model accuracy in 0.1-wide bins reveals momentum obscured by ceiling effects. Corrected hierarchical variance estimators subtract uncertainty in finetuning averages, while Gaussian-process curves compare variance conditional on squared bias. Across settings, finetuning variance is reported as 2–8 times pretraining variance; other size-ordering claims require qualifications. The paper frames predictions as data to mine, recommends sharing them alongside weights, and reports releasing checkpoints, predictions, and code.
attribution_limits: The research framing, statistical revisions, recommendations, and reported results belong to the collaboration. The paper specifically assigns annotation to the first and second authors, not Steinhardt; its replication is internal and qualitative, not an external validation or full agreement study. Neither methodological changes nor counterfactual savings establish Steinhardt's individual actions or personal philosophy. Artifact release is reported, not independently checked.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Ensembling repairs the relevant independence structure but changes the prediction procedure being studied. The bootstrap population is the empirical distribution of ten checkpoints; it does not provide a universal bias guarantee. Prose calls threshold-selection bias at most around 10%, whereas the table includes 0.149 and 0.146, approaching 15%. Conditional momentum is positive in nearly all—not all—appendix buckets, with some zero or negative entries. Large has lower pretraining variance than base, but rankings among other sizes vary with task and loss. Conditional finetuning-variance trends also have exceptions, including medium versus mini on SST-2. Label-quality adjustments depend on sampled human judgments, and statistical evidence of regressions does not explain their linguistic mechanism.
coverage_notes: Repeated extractions describe one project. MNLI reserves 50,000 of 400,000 training examples for evaluation; SST-2 uses five-fold evaluation on combined training/development data. Four-epoch finetuning uses task/size-specific selection among nine batch-size/learning-rate combinations on an internal 80/20 split. Reported compute is approximately 3,840 pretraining hours on eight-core TPU v3 hardware plus 1,200 finetuning hours. Predictions also cover SNLI, HANS, stress tests, and TwitterPPDB, but main conclusions are not thereby established on every dataset. Main comparisons involve at most three sizes. The appendix extends variance estimation to checkpoints and unequal randomness trees with at least two children per nonterminal node, using unbiased component estimators. Metadata-guided subgroup discovery and links to probing or language-model loss remain proposals, not achieved explanations.

substance:
This project investigates how input-distribution structure and explicit labels jointly shape last-layer representations. It challenges the explanatory reach, rather than the mathematical validity, of unconstrained-feature models: removing input dependence prevents them from explaining retained subclass organization. The experimental intervention keeps images fixed while merging CIFAR-10 classes into five coarse labels or randomly splitting each original class into two, producing twenty fine labels. Original classes operationalize input structure, not a uniquely established intrinsic taxonomy. Deterministic modulo-based merging was chosen for simplicity and reproducibility, with random merging checked separately.

Before interpreting residual structure, the authors verify coarse-label Neural Collapse through NC1 and NC2, including five clusters whose means approach a simplex equiangular tight frame. Average squared-distance matrices and within-superclass t-SNE plots reveal finer distinctions: original-class organization appears earlier than training-label structure and can survive after zero training error. Fine CIFAR-10 likewise initially reflects ten rather than twenty clusters, with traces remaining later. Extending training to 1,000 epochs tests—and supports—finite-duration persistence, not asymptotic persistence.

The Cluster-and-Linear-Probe test turns visual evidence into a functional measurement. Two-dimensional t-SNE followed by two-means clustering within each coarse class reconstructs labels; a linear probe trained using these labels is evaluated on original CIFAR-10. The method assumes the subclass count and reports the best cluster-to-class permutation, alongside true-label probing and ordinary training comparisons. Approximately 93% test accuracy suggests that small residual variations retain substantial predictive information, but does not demonstrate autonomous recovery of semantic class names.

Boundary tests complicate generalization. With CIFAR-100's twenty natural superclasses, ResNet-18 does not separate every subclass: bicycles and motorcycles are entangled, as are crabs and lobsters, while more dissimilar subclasses separate better. Random groupings separate more clearly. DenseNet-121 supports the main observations, whereas VGG-18 shows collapse without distinguishing original subclasses even early in training; the cause remains unresolved.

The theory deliberately studies a shallow network on four Gaussian clusters with orthogonal means, two coarse labels, fixed second-layer weights, and restrictive training conditions. Its mechanism is stronger neuron alignment with shared cluster means than individual-sample noise. The proof uses unhinged loss and controls a cubic-activation regime; the stated logistic extension relies on small outputs. Analogous—not identical—synthetic experiments use eight clusters of 500 examples, 1,000 gradient steps, and ten-run averages. Their between-/within-subclass squared-distance ratio increases with input and hidden dimensions; weight decay has no observed effect there. Controlled cluster similarity also supports a need for sufficient subclass separation.
attribution_limits: All interventions, findings, proof strategies, and deferrals are collective research evidence. No excerpt independently identifies Steinhardt as originating a particular experiment or expressing an individual preference. Temporal claims describe representation learning, not changes in researchers' beliefs. The theorem is restricted to its synthetic assumptions and does not prove the behavior of ResNet, DenseNet, or CIFAR models. The supplied excerpts describe the proof without independently validating it.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Residual structure is not universal: VGG-18 is an explicit unresolved counterexample, and naturally similar subclasses can remain inseparable. Neural Collapse and useful residual variation coexist at different scales, so the findings do not simply refute collapse. Image experiments show learning-rate and weight-decay dependence even though synthetic MSDR is insensitive to weight decay. Best-permutation CLP scoring and supplied subclass counts limit claims of unsupervised label recovery. Two low-learning-rate configurations retain training error below 0.5% rather than exactly zero; six grid configurations reach zero, while the highest-learning-rate/highest-decay combination is another convergence exception. Thus not every plotted run is equally evidence about a zero-error terminal phase.
coverage_notes: Repeated records are overlapping accounts of the same project. The image grid combines learning rates 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 with weight decays 0.005, 0.0005, and 0.00005; 'exhaustive' means this finite grid. Synthetic one-factor sweeps hold other settings at input dimension 512, hidden dimension 512, and zero weight decay. Geometric proximity in Gaussian mixtures is an analogue, not a full measurement, of semantic similarity. The number of independently sampled random class permutations and uncertainty intervals for synthetic averages are not established by the excerpts. Architecture and optimization dependencies are explicitly deferred for further study.

substance:
The project seeks a measurable constructive target for interpretability: can visualizations reveal deliberately altered model behavior? Its 'counterauditing' framework separates detecting an unusual model from localizing inputs on which it behaves unusually. Localization means ranking affected examples, not identifying causal pixels or repairing a network. Twelve ImageNet ResNet-50 reference models share training hyperparameters but differ by seed. Twenty-four anomalous models span randomized smoothing, adversarial training, shape bias, backdoors, spurious features, missing classes, and blurred-face training; anomalous does not necessarily mean malicious or undesirable.

Anomaly scores divide candidate-to-reference visualization distances by reference-to-reference variation. The main distance is AlexNet-based LPIPS, with VGG and SqueezeNet variants checked. Attribution methods use established libraries and largely default settings; Caricatures use 512 Lucent optimization steps. Seven layers sample different network stages and residual-block positions while limiting computation. Model detection requires a score averaged over fifty images to exceed every reference model's score; Caricature detection additionally averages layers.

The interventions include class-index overlays on 100%, 50%, 30%, or 10% of training images, and six backdoors with little clean-accuracy loss but near-zero accuracy on triggered inputs. Under the main metric, Caricatures detect all backdoors but only one quarter of spurious-feature models; Integrated Gradients detects all spurious-feature models but only 17% of backdoors. No method detects missing-class or blurred-face models in that main setup. Illustrative visual inspections corroborate selected successes and failures, without constituting a human-subject study.

Localization is restricted to four anomaly families with known affected subsets. Forty normal and forty abnormal images yield AUROC scores; under the exchangeability null, 0.4–0.6 is indistinguishable from chance at this sample size. Only 31% of reported scores exceed the adopted 0.7 acceptability convention, while 54% lie near chance. Missing-class tests have only two of thirty-three scores above 0.7. Stronger cue exposure does not reliably improve localization: Integrated Gradients scores 0.42 at full exposure. A Caricature layer's blurred-face AUROC of 0.28 remains unexplained, and a spatial-region explanation for attribution successes fails to explain spurious-cue weaknesses.

The authors deliberately interpret easy tests asymmetrically: failure challenges sensitivity, while passing gives limited reassurance. References vary only by seed, half the backdoors poison 30–50% of training data, and affected inputs are supplied rather than discovered. They propose specification-based evaluation without normal-model references and evaluation of input-independent transparency methods, but implement neither extension here.
attribution_limits: The quantifiable-goal preference, counterauditing rationale, surprise, and proposed extensions are expressed collectively by Denain and Steinhardt. The excerpts do not isolate individual authorship or personal preferences. Reported results concern specific implementations, reference models, samples, and perceptual metrics, not every interpretability method or all debugging utility. LPIPS robustness checks are not direct validation against human judgments.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Exact detection fractions change with the LPIPS backbone; some alternative-metric appendix entries detect individual missing-class or blurred-face cases. The stark/subtle taxonomy is approximate: full spurious-cue exposure materially harms ordinary validation accuracy, while some adversarial conditions have weak effects. Internally trained anomaly families share controls, but external checkpoints do not all match: the shape-biased model uses 60 rather than 90 epochs, different batch size, and different learning-rate milestones. Similar normal-model accuracy by epoch 60 does not eliminate representation confounds. Failure to detect class removal only suggests, rather than proves, small feature changes or feature sharing. Related work finds poorer backdoor localization under more sophisticated attacks and different evaluation definitions; the cause of disagreement is not isolated.
coverage_notes: Duplicate extractions are not independent evidence. Missing classes include academic gown and backpack sampled from all classes, plus Welsh springer spaniel sampled from dog classes because abundant related dog categories were expected to make removal harder to detect.
