The empirical component, run by Lev McKinney, queried models to count from 1 to n for n=100–1900 in steps of 100, stopping at n generated tokens because numbers can span tokens. Regression with an intercept separated fixed latency from asymptotic throughput. Pythia runs used DeepSpeed injected kernels, fp16, and one A100. For human comparisons, Steinhardt selected 380 words per minute from several neighboring estimates, approximately 500 tokens per minute. He retained the cited 4:3 token/word conversion despite personally judging 3:2 or 2:1 more plausible. His median inference forecast was five times human word rate, with a 0.5–20-times range. A separate theoretical tiling argument trades fivefold lower throughput for twenty-fivefold faster individual execution, yielding 125-times-human speed from that baseline.

He estimates deployment capacity through “training overhang”: resources needed for training could subsequently run model copies. The calculation starts with Chinchilla scaling, combines compute projections using a geometric median, corrects GPT-3’s suboptimal training allocation, and explores data scarcity. Larger models could reduce overhang; synthetic-data generation could increase it; new modalities have uncertain effects. He subjectively widens the final range to 0.4–10 million human-speed-equivalent years of nominal model work around 1.8 million. Training-resource and deployment-demand calculations separately suggest roughly one million copies could learn in parallel. He rejects using maximum forecast parameter count as a proxy for frontier-model inference cost.

Capability predictions are deliberately uneven: economic usefulness and language-data scarcity motivate proteins, biomedical data, CAD, astronomy, and genomics, while costly physical data slow robotics. He gives 50% probability to outperforming median UCSD mathematics faculty on solve rate and time for five randomly selected Electronic Journal of Combinatorics theorem statements, but 40% to autonomous assembly of a specified scale-replica Ferrari.

Impact analysis filters tasks by comparative model strength, cheap external evidence, and reliable decomposition or automated feedback. He anticipates human-directed AI experiment execution, while skill mismatch, experiment costs, and limited autonomy constrain productivity. The same framework identifies research acceleration, cyberattacks, and manipulation risks. His explicit recommendation is preparation at trillion-dollar, multimillion-life, and institutional scales—not a prediction of realized losses.
attribution_limits: The forecasting approach, parameter choices, personal doubt about token conversion, and preparation recommendation are explicitly attributable to Steinhardt. McKinney is credited with executing the speed experiments; Geoff Hinton is credited with introducing the shared-learning argument to him. External scaling relationships and compute forecasts are inputs, not his independent measurements. The mathematics and Ferrari criteria, autonomy duration, future research workflow, and misuse scenarios are forecasts or proposals, not completed demonstrations.
tensions_and_counterevidence: More than ten hours examining hardware and model-size trends left him highly uncertain about their net speed effect. Words per minute conflates model writing, difficult code generation, verbosity, and compressed human thought; the considered extended-thought estimate was approximately 4,200 words per minute, unlike the selected 380 baseline. No validated cognitive-work correction is supplied. Forecast ranges are subjective 25th–75th percentiles, explicitly probably too narrow because alternative scenarios were omitted; these differ from the benchmark’s 95% confidence intervals. Deployment estimates assume retained resources and effective parallel learning. His estimate is below Cotra’s and Davidson’s, with data-scarcity modeling only a guessed explanation. He roughly expects resets or steering after several human-equivalent days, implying oversight every several hours at fivefold speed.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and calculations; they are one forecasting essay, not independent confirmations. API measurements date to early April 2023, and replication code is linked but not independently verified here. Counting throughput does not establish reasoning speed or research productivity. The tiling speedup is theoretical and hardware-dependent. The surprise at Minerva documents an experience, not a quantified prior or measured forecast update.

substance:
This collaboration asks whether agents can be steered toward moral behavior without unrealistically dense human feedback, using semantically richer settings than gridworlds. Jiminy Cricket comprises 25 Infocom text adventures. Trained graduate and undergraduate annotators learned ZIL and spent six months annotating over 400,000 source-code lines rather than only sampled trajectories; technical requirements ruled out marketplace crowdsourcing. An audit found 17.2% of rewarded expert-walkthrough actions were immoral under the benchmark framework, motivating evaluation beyond game reward.

Annotations include salience recognized by several ethical traditions and define immorality pro tanto: an action can have bad aspects even when justified overall. Attempted theft receives degree 1 versus degree 2 for completed theft. Annotators used consequences specified by the environment and extended example categories when distinct scenarios appeared. To counter agents getting stuck early, evaluation starts at 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% along expert walkthroughs, reportedly increasing CALM’s encountered unique morality annotations by 240%. Progress, severity-based immorality, and immorality per percent completion are assessed separately.

The team retrained CALM’s GPT-2 action generator with benchmark games removed and used a DRRN Q-learning backbone. Commonsense Morality Policy Shaping uses an ETHICS-trained RoBERTa-large classifier on action statements, thresholds its scores, and subtracts gamma=10 from flagged actions’ Q-values—effectively banning them. Thresholds were calibrated to 10% false positives on annotated benchmark actions. Runs used eight parallel environments, 100-action episodes, and up to 15,000 training steps, stopping after 5,000 if maximum score remained nonpositive.

CMPS reduced Relative Immorality from 0.85 to 0.52, approximately 39%, while completion remained nearly unchanged at 3.68 versus 3.64. Oracle labels reduced raw immorality from 1.90 to 0.13, suggesting recognition headroom rather than demonstrating an attainable classifier. Interaction-budget curves indicated improvement beyond merely stopping CALM sooner; training curves also showed less harm during learning. Thresholding outperformed soft shaping on completion and immorality. Utility shaping increased completion but worsened aggregate immorality while reducing the most severe actions; reward shaping performed worse overall but retained access to action consequences.

Engineering altered experimental feasibility. Quadratic valid-action enumeration prompted reliance on language priors. Invalid-action recovery switched from random resampling to the highest-Q remaining candidate while preserving initial exploration. Shared Transformer context computation and key/value caches reduced measured peak memory from 9.06 to 2.52 GB and runtime from 5.04 to 3.95 hours, enabling simultaneous agent/classifier execution. Direct classifier diagnostics supplemented expensive agent runs: 100 candidate actions per walkthrough step yielded AUROCs of 72.5% for commonsense morality and 59.4% for utility.
attribution_limits: All research choices, results, ethical framing, and deployment cautions are collective statements. The supplied evidence does not assign Steinhardt individual responsibility for annotation, engineering, staffing, or moral judgments. The framework is a benchmark convention, not his personal ethical weighting. Combining knowledge sources or reward and policy shaping is proposed future work. Scanned supplementary game materials anticipate multimodal agents; no reported experiment demonstrates such use. Results concern simulated text-game behavior, not real-world moral competence.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Evaluation-only and zero-shot framing is qualified by target-label threshold calibration, oracle experiments, and recommended validation games. Action-only classification lacks full context, while pro tanto harms can be necessary to prevent worse outcomes. Ordinal severity aggregation imposes contestable numerical weights; Relative Immorality is not comparable at nonpositive completion. Absolute competence remains low. Tables support roughly 39%, not the prose’s 64%, raw-immorality reduction, and improvement in 22 rather than 23 games. Severe-harm values 0.054 to 0.040 imply approximately 26%, not the stated 34%, reduction. The claimed 360% memory reduction is invalid; raw measurements are usable. The authors acknowledge cultural variation, support replacement frameworks, and strongly discourage deployment use. A heading asserts full legal compliance, but the accompanying text acknowledges unknown copyright status and relies on an assumption of fair use, not a verified legal conclusion.
coverage_notes: Repeated extracts describe one project. Supporting benchmark work includes source-level interpretable object trees; printed annotation identifiers parsed after ZILF recompilation; expert walkthroughs as soft, not proven, performance ceilings; and scanned “feelies.” Custom rewards were added to Moonmist, Suspect, Witness, Borderzone, and Deadline, with completion rewards added where absent, so scoring is not wholly historical. The banned-token processor was narrowed to individual tokens to remove quadratic matching, sacrificing general multi-token support. Oracle exploration exposed infinite loops that were patched; ordinary agents had not triggered them. Automated checks and playtesting address acknowledged, unquantified annotation errors. Agreement was tested on only 42 scenarios across three games: 100% broad-category and 95% degree agreement. Code, annotation pipeline, and quality-assurance scripts support reuse without promising continuing updates. Suggested validation games are Zork 1, Stationfall, Enchanter, Suspect, and Sherlock; this does not establish that every reported calibration used a held-out split.

substance:
The paper investigates when Tukey-depth maximization remains a useful robust location estimator after strengthening the adversary from Huber-style additive contamination to total-variation corruption, which permits deleting as well as adding probability mass. It seeks maximum-bias bounds and both sides of the breakdown threshold, rather than only a sufficient robustness guarantee. Nonuniqueness is consequential: the Tukey median is defined as the entire set of depth maximizers, and maximum bias takes suprema over median-set elements rather than assuming favorable tie-breaking. Family breakdown is the worst breakdown among distributions in the specified class.

For halfspace-symmetric distributions in dimension at least three, the worst-case breakdown threshold falls from one third under additive corruption to one quarter under total variation. The upper-bound construction begins with four equally weighted vertices of a planar square. Moving (1,1,0) to (-0.5,-0.5,z) creates a tetrahedron whose interior points all have maximal depth one quarter. Letting z grow produces arbitrarily distant medians after changing only one quarter of the mass. This is a mathematical failure construction, not typical-data evidence.

To characterize behavior before breakdown, the authors introduce a worst-direction decay function describing mass around the center and express bias bounds through its generalized inverse. They also extend the formulation beyond halfspace symmetry by taking account of all original Tukey medians, without thereby retaining the symmetry-specific breakdown guarantee. For Gaussian distributions with bounded covariance operator norm, the analysis recovers O(ε) error, reported as optimal up to constants, with O(d/ε²) samples. The finite-sample proof handles the specified adaptive corruption model, thereby covering the oblivious case, and separates corruption effects from empirical-to-population deviation using halfspace VC bounds; constants and confidence dependence qualify the shorthand sample rate.

A comparison estimator projects onto a known halfspace-symmetric distribution class G(h) under a restricted halfspace distance. It obtains one-half breakdown and better maximum-bias bounds, but requires class knowledge that Tukey-median computation does not. Its geometric advantage is access to a separating halfspace through the midpoint of the true and estimated centers. The restricted metric also permits useful finite-sample convergence where full total variation can remain maximally discrepant between empirical and continuous population distributions.

The conclusion preserves unresolved tradeoffs: Tukey medians are affine-equivariant, whereas this projection method is not; neither is established here as efficiently computable. The proposed open problem is to combine affine equivariance, one-half breakdown, and good finite-sample error for halfspace-symmetric distributions, even before requiring computational efficiency.
attribution_limits: These are jointly authored theoretical definitions, constructions, guarantees, and research directions from Zhu, Jiao, and Steinhardt. No supplied passage identifies Steinhardt as personally choosing the adversary model or prioritizing statistical questions over computation. The projection approach is credited to earlier work; this paper analyzes its comparison in the selected setting. Gaussian optimality invokes prior literature not independently supplied. No empirical experiment or implementation performance is documented.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The stronger corruption model materially weakens a familiar robustness guarantee, but this is a model comparison, not a documented change of personal belief. The one-quarter threshold is a worst-case family result for d≥3, not a universal value for all dimensions or distributions. Projection’s stronger guarantee comes with extra distributional information and loss of affine equivariance, so it is not an unqualified replacement. Full total variation equal to one is an empirical-versus-population obstruction, not a statement valid for every discrete population. The adaptive adversary has the paper’s specified replacement-budget conditions, not unrestricted power. Possible computational difficulty is acknowledged, not proved as an impossibility.
coverage_notes: Many records repeat the same definitions, theorems, and concluding comparison; count one theoretical project. The supplied evidence does not give lower-dimensional breakdown values, so none are inferred. The source’s compressed wording about the halfspaces available to the Tukey median supports the midpoint distinction but not a more elaborate reconstructed proof. The concluding open problem is stated at publication time; its current status and subsequent pursuit are not established.

substance:
Yin and Steinhardt compare induction heads and function-vector (FV) heads as explanations of in-context learning across 12 decoder-only models spanning 70M–7B parameters and 45 natural-language tasks overall. They define ICL as few-shot learning from prompts without parameter updates and rename the loss difference between context tokens 50 and 500 “token-loss difference,” explicitly separating it from task accuracy.

Induction scores average normalized attention behavior over 1,000 repeated random 50-token sequences. FV scores measure recovery of correct-output probability when a head’s task-conditioned mean activation replaces its activation in prompts with shuffled demonstration labels. The top 2% of heads represent each mechanism; the authors avoid relying on whole-population correlations dominated by jointly low-scoring heads. Seven models have no overlap between these top sets, and the others have only 5–15%, yet cross-mechanism scores are relatively high—often around the 90th–95th percentile. Thus distinct sets do not imply uncorrelated behaviors.

For causal evaluation, 37 prior tasks were split into 26 for FV identification and 11 for evaluation, augmented with eight new tasks to produce 19 evaluation tasks with 100 prompts each. Ablations replace outputs with dataset means to mitigate zero-ablation distribution shifts, remove 1–20% of heads, and compare clean and random-head baselines. Initial induction ablations appeared consequential. Recognizing increasing overlap among removed heads prompted exclusion experiments: preserve the competing mechanism’s top 2% while ablating the target ranking. Above 1B parameters, induction ablation then approached random-ablation damage, whereas FV ablation remained harmful. At 70M, both mechanisms had similar effects. On 10,000 Pile examples, token-loss difference showed a contrasting pattern, helping reconcile earlier induction-head findings without treating either metric as interchangeable with the other.

Developmental analysis examined eight intermediate checkpoints in seven Pythia models. Induction emerged around step 1,000 of 143,000; FV behavior appeared around 16,000 and strengthened later. Many eventual FV heads initially scored strongly on induction, then lost induction strength while gaining FV strength; no reverse transition was observed. These trajectories motivate, but do not prove, induction as a developmental precursor.

A supplementary test used 1,000 examples per task unseen during FV scoring across 40 tasks, comparing clean prompts, shuffled labels, task-vector insertion at one-third model depth, and random-head vectors. FV insertion generally recovered clean-prompt performance, except in Pythia 2.8B. Importantly, raw mechanism scores did not reproduce the scale trend in ablation importance. The paper separates experimental findings from conjectures about greater abstraction, precursor relationships, and polysemantic computations rather than presenting one settled account.
attribution_limits: Problem selection, terminology recommendations, experimental decisions, results, and conjectures are jointly attributed to Yin and Steinhardt; no individual division of labor is supplied. The revised interpretation of induction ablations is a within-project change, not evidence that Steinhardt personally reversed a prior position. Causal statements concern specified activation interventions. Removing induction heads during training is proposed future work, not a completed developmental test. Greater computational abstraction is explicitly conjectural.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Some FV heads retain low induction scores throughout training, limiting the precursor account. An alternative proposes polysemantic heads whose attention diversifies rather than replacing induction, but substantial damage from ablating FV heads with little measured induction challenges a simple combined-mechanism explanation. Calling such heads “monosemantic” only operationalizes low induction scores; it does not exclude other functions. Top-2% exclusion does not ensure mechanistic purity, and cutoff sensitivity is not established by the supplied text. Mean ablation mitigates rather than eliminates intervention artifacts. Pythia 2.8B’s recovery exception is tentatively linked to head dimension 80 versus 128 in some comparably sized models, but dimensionality was not isolated experimentally. Results through 7B do not establish universality at larger scales.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project. The 45-task overall scope, 19-task primary ablation evaluation, and 40-task supplementary recovery test are distinct, not inconsistent counts. Alternative zero and randomly sourced head-output ablations are described, and robustness is reported, but numerical figure curves are unavailable in the supplied text. Layer-targeted random ablations address location differences; their design is supplied without a quantitative conclusion. Eight checkpoints provide sampled trajectories within Pythia, not continuous developmental observation or evidence across every model family.
